n: Israel sins again, and the Lord gives them over to Midian, desert nomads from east of the Jordan, for seven years.

f.g: Descendants of Abraham through Keturah; Moses had married into a Midianite family.

n: Midian’s raids were so harsh that Israelites hid in mountain caves and strongholds.

f.g: Hiding places, perhaps cut into hillsides.

n: Each year after planting, the Midianites, Amalekites, and other eastern tribes swept in to take the harvest.

f.g: Desert tribes from east of the Jordan.

n: They camped on the land and ate or destroyed everything as far as Gaza, leaving no food or livestock.

f.g: Crops, produce.
Food.

n: They came like locusts with their camels and herds — too many to count. This is one of the first records of camels used in large-scale raiding.

f.g: Locusts, which strip a land bare.

n: Israel is reduced to poverty and finally cries out to the Lord.

f.g: Brought very low.

n: Israel’s cry is repeated to show it reached God.
Before sending a deliverer, God sends an unnamed prophet to explain why this happened. He begins by recalling the Exodus.

f.g: An unnamed prophet; God first sends correction, then rescue.

n: God reminds them He rescued them from Egypt and every oppressor and gave them the land.

f.g: Drove them out.

n: God had told them not to fear the Amorites’ gods, but they disobeyed. Recognizing sin comes before deliverance.

f.w: fear not the gods of the Amorites

n: The angel of the Lord sits under an oak at Ophrah while Gideon secretly threshes wheat in a winepress — a pit where the grain would be hidden from raiders.

f.g: Threshing was normally done on open hilltops to catch the wind; a winepress was a sunken pit, good for hiding.

n: The angel greets him as a “mighty man of valour” — not what he was, but what God saw he could become.
Gideon answers honestly: if God is with us, why is this happening? Where are the miracles our fathers told us about? Scripture allows sincere questions.
The speaker is now called “the LORD.” He doesn’t argue; He sends: “Go in this thy might… have not I sent thee?” God’s call is His answer.

f.g: The angel speaks as the Lord Himself; Latter-day Saints understand Jehovah as the premortal Christ.

n: Gideon protests that his clan is the weakest in Manasseh and he is the least in his family. God often calls the humble.

f.w: I am the least in my father's house

f.g: With what? How?

n: God promises His presence: Gideon will strike Midian as easily as one man.

f.w: Surely I will be with thee

n: Gideon asks for a sign that he is truly speaking with God.

f.g: Found favor with you.

n: He begs the visitor to wait while he brings an offering, and the visitor agrees.

f.g: A gift or offering.
Wait.

n: Gideon prepares a young goat, broth, and unleavened bread from about a bushel of flour — a costly gift in a time of famine.

f.g: Young goat.
A dry measure, roughly 20 liters (about half a bushel).

n: The angel tells him to set the food on a rock and pour out the broth, turning the meal into an offering.

f.g: Another title for the same divine messenger.

n: With a touch of his staff, fire flares from the rock and consumes the offering, and the angel vanishes. God accepts the sacrifice.

f.w: there rose up fire out of the rock

n: Gideon realizes who he has seen and is terrified, fearing that no one sees God face to face and lives.
The Lord comforts him: “Peace be unto thee; fear not.”
Gideon builds an altar and names it “The LORD is peace.” The altar still stood when the book was written.

f.g: “The LORD is peace.”

n: That night God gives Gideon his first mission: tear down his own father’s Baal altar and the Asherah pole beside it. Reform starts at home.

f.g: An Asherah pole, a wooden cult object.

f.w: the second bullock of seven years old
f.g: Seven years may echo the seven years of Midianite oppression.

n: He is to build a proper altar to the Lord and burn the bull using the wood of the Asherah pole.

f.g: In proper arrangement, or on the stronghold’s top.

n: Gideon obeys — but at night, afraid of his family and neighbors. His courage is real, if still growing.
In the morning the town sees the Baal altar destroyed and a new altar in use.

f.g: Torn down.

n: They investigate and learn Gideon did it.

f.g: Shows how deeply Baal worship had taken root in an Israelite town.

n: Shockingly, Israelites demand death for destroying Baal’s altar — the reverse of God’s law, which condemned idolaters.
Joash defends his son with sharp logic: if Baal is a god, let him defend himself. Gideon’s faith may have awakened his father’s.

f.w: if he be a god, let him plead for himself

n: Gideon is nicknamed Jerubbaal, “let Baal contend,” a standing mockery of Baal’s powerlessness.

f.g: “Let Baal contend (against him).”

n: The Midianite coalition crosses the Jordan and camps in the Jezreel valley.

f.g: Israel’s richest farmland, a natural target.

n: The Spirit of the Lord “clothes” Gideon. He blows the trumpet, and his own clan, which had wanted him dead, rallies to him.

f.w: the Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon
f.g: Literally “clothed itself with Gideon.”

n: Gideon summons Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they come.
Gideon, still uncertain, asks God for confirmation.
He sets out a wool fleece on the threshing floor: let dew fall only on the fleece, and the ground stay dry.

f.g: A sheepskin with the wool still on.
Threshing floor.

n: God grants it: by morning Gideon wrings a full bowl of water from the fleece.

f.g: Squeezed out.

n: Gideon humbly asks again, this time reversing the sign, since wool naturally holds dew.

f.w: Let not thine anger be hot against me

n: God patiently does it: the fleece is dry and the ground wet. The Lord meets Gideon in his weakness — though faith grows best when we act without demanding more signs.
